## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nigrodhajātaka* (Ja 445) is a narrative included in the Pali Jātaka collection. The frame story takes place at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) near Rājagaha and concerns Devadatta [Fausböll 1887]. When fellow monks remind Devadatta of his profound debt to the Buddha—having received ordination, mastered the Three Baskets, and attained meditative absorption through him—Devadatta ungratefully dismisses the Teacher by picking up a blade of grass and claiming the Buddha did not even do that much good for him [Fausböll 1887]. In response, the Buddha remarks that Devadatta was similarly ungrateful and treacherous to his friends in previous lives, and relates the story of the past [Fausböll 1887].

The past story illustrates deeds as seeds and the virtue of gratitude: three boys receive an education—two rich and one poor—with the poor boy's fees sponsored by the first; later, when the poor boy discovers how to obtain kingship, he bestows it on his benefactor [Anandajoti 2010]. In the story's verse and concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Bodhisatta is identified as Nigrodha, Ānanda as Poṭṭika, and Devadatta as Sākha [Fausböll 1887].

 Computational analysis by DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse across nine segments with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo), as well as low-level machine alignments with the Sanskrit *Āryasaṃghāṭasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
